Our analysis challenges the current trend of using the Thakurta metric to study primordial black holes. This characterisation assumes that the singular part of these black holes remains unchanged up to the cosmological scale. However, our findings suggest that the singular part should be limited to the event horizon, leading to a revised estimation of primordial black hole masses and radii that is largely consistent with existing constraints from the LIGO-Virgo collaboration. This change in approach has no impact on the estimates of the fraction of primordial black holes in relation to dark matter within the LIGO-Virgo area of study, as they remain predominantly below 10\% despite changes in the model.

The formation of planets through pebble accretion on protoplanetary disks relies heavily on how efficiently solid material is incorporated into the disk and dispersed as pebbles. To determine the limitations of this theory, we simulated open clusters to model the real-world effects of density fluctuations. Our findings suggest that a uniform distribution of pebbles is insufficient to explain the formation of planets. We found that density fluctuations within pebble layers play a crucial role in guiding the growth of planets and influence the type of planetary masses formed. Specifically, areas with high pebble layer density contribute more to the growth of planets than those with low pebble layers. Additionally, we discovered that density fluctuations impact the mass range of planets formed, with denser regions producing planets with greater mass. Our simulations also indicate that planets form more easily in areas with uniform or oscillating pebble layer densities. Conversely, planets have a lower chance of forming in areas with rapidly changing or inconsistent pebble layer densities.

We investigate how the computational burdens of training and evaluating deep neural networks affect their performance. Two new theoretical insights illuminate the connection between a model's complexity and its ability to accurately predict its behavior. First, models with a large number of parameters don't necessarily need to overfit if they can efficiently evaluate previous predictions. However, when predicting new, unseen data becomes computationally challenging, a model may tend to overfit even if it can train efficiently. Secondly, our research reveals that the risk of a model overfitting can also be heightened if the model is extremely large and there is no shortcut to quickly evaluate its performance using approximate methods. This finding is supported by our analysis of a simple binary classification task and a real-world dataset, as well as visualizations of a model's loss surface under different training conditions.

In a prior study, it was demonstrated that for any real number c, there exists an infinite sequence of natural numbers with the property that the sum of any two numbers from the sequence never equals another sum of two numbers from the sequence, and the sum of any n such numbers exceeds the product of the sums multiplied by a constant depending on n, but this constant can be made arbitrarily small by selecting a sufficiently large n. Assuming the sequence is chosen from a finite group, and adding the condition that the sum of any n such numbers exceeds c times the product of the sums, it is proven that the sequence satisfies an additive Bohr structure, and the number on the right can be set to 1 plus the reciprocal of n. This solution can be applied to combinatorial number theory, and it may provide alternatives to the sum of squares problem and the APO, all of which bear similarities to the problem we have solved.

The dial-a-ride problem with a large number of passengers appears to be an unsolved issue even with the application of exact methods, mainly due to the presence of complementary choices and seat constraints on vehicles. To address this challenge, a new exact algorithm is presented, targeted at small to moderate-sized problems involving up to 200 passengers and ten vehicles. This method features a rapid evaluation of non-negative solutions using a reduced set of linear constraints derived from the problem solution branch. Comprehensive computational experiments were conducted with increasingly trimmed sets until a non-negative solution is found that fulfils all passengers' requirements. Our study examines various trimming strategies and sets, including those derived from QP-based solutions for a related problem variant. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, which successfully solves a significant proportion of instances within reasonable computational time and also allows to tackle previously unsolved instances with high precision using a branch-and-cut branch-and-terminate method that combines branch-and-cut with cuts derived from conic relaxations for laminar graphs.

In e-commerce, visual data like images and videos are crucial for product interaction recognition but have limitations in providing comprehensive information due to the lack of knowledge integration. To address this issue, we developed a multi-modal pretraining method that combines image and text data with knowledge-based embedding for robust product interaction recognition. Our method utilizes BERT to create a joint embedding space for multi-modal inputs and knowledge integration. The model incorporates an attention mechanism to balance end-to-end trained image-text, image-knowledge, and text-knowledge features. The knowledge integration enables more accurate representations of difficult-to-observe interactions like comparisons during novel category recognition. Experimental results on real datasets reveal that our proposed approach significantly outperforms existing methods in e-commerce product interaction recognition, particularly in comparison tasks.

One of the primary concerns associated with aging is Alzheimer's disease, a progressive condition characterized by cognitive decline and memory loss. It's estimated that approximately 10% of people aged 65 and over are diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease, a statistic that's likely to rise as the global population ages. Early detection and intervention of the disease can significantly improve patient outcomes and overall quality of life, making accurate forecasting essential. Our research focuses on developing a forecasting model for tracking Alzheimer's progression using Deep InfoMax, a technique that utilizes maximum-entropy representations to encode variable relationships. Our approach is based on a comprehensive analysis of MRI images, clinical data, and baseline cognitive scores from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. By integrating deep neural networks, our model outperforms current standards in forecasting and provides robust generative capabilities, outperforming existing methods in both discriminative and generative tasks.

Natural Language Processing has been successfully applied across various domains, and a task that draws significant attention is sentiment analysis. However, machine learning models' performance in this area face challenges due to sentiment ambiguity and nuances, as well as complex sentence structures. Despite the development of linear and non-linear models based on deep learning, achieving high accuracy while handling diverse sentiment expressions remains a difficult task. In this research, a novel interaction-driven recurrent neural network architecture is introduced for sentiment analysis, addressing the problem of sentence sentence sentence through character-level recurrent neural networks. The model's key innovation is its ability to incorporate external knowledge from a semantic dictionary to inform sentiment interpretation, thus enhancing the ability to capture subtle sentiment cues. Experimental findings reveal that the proposed architecture achieves high accuracy while effectively handling diverse sentiment expressions.

The effectiveness of spin-orbit interaction in materials with high electron interaction strengths is a significant issue in theory and material science. Through a screening process, we eliminate the issue that arises in traditional models, thereby making effective spin-orbit interaction achievable in these environments. By considering its influence, we obtain an improved estimate of the reduction resulting from strong electron interaction within a two-dimensional semiconductor material. Furthermore, our findings are also relevant to other materials with strong spin-orbit coupling and high electron interaction strengths.

In this paper, we make a distinction between a body's inherent appearance, 
its material properties, and how these properties are perceived, which of which 
can be considered the simplest, most fundamental form. A novel model, 
the Shadow Substance, is introduced which has the same external appearance 
as a given body but its internal properties and behavior can differ. This 
concept is then used to develop the Metastable Conformal Shadow Substance, 
a specific type of Shadow Substance, which maintains specific proportions of 
material properties, like density and refractive index, in relation to 
a corresponding body. This type of Shadow Substance is unique in its 
characteristics and is useful for redefining and applying certain concepts 
in a more straightforward manner. A key application of this is in the 
Metastable conformal doping of Liquids.

Medical imaging AI models, deployed as medical devices, are expected to maintain high performance levels when faced with typical variations in patient data. However, they often struggle when encountering more significant domain shifts. Without an established standard for evaluating medical device AI, the effectiveness of these models is usually tested under a limited set of patient characteristics. Since medical imaging AI models operate on complex image data, a lack of methodological work in this area has hindered researchers and developers from fully exploring their potential. To bridge this gap, this research proposes an approach to assess medical imaging AI models under various types of domain shifts, utilizing conformal forecasting. This method provides a level of confidence in its results, along with an expandable framework for evaluating these models under diverse shift conditions, which can serve as a useful template for future research.

Molecular dynamics simulations may fall short by failing to account for certain conformational changes due to the dynamic nature of residue interactions. We challenge this approach in simulations of double-stranded DNA by introducing a fixed interaction bias that emulates the effects of chemical modifications that stabilize certain conformations. This "stiff base" potential can be applied as an additive correction with well-established parameters or by using a simple procedure to reassign the base repulsion parameters. Through small system tests, we demonstrate improved DNA conformational sampling that is comparable to machine-learning-based potential systems. This "stiff base" approach offers an efficient and straightforward way to enhance the accuracy of DNA-based simulation models.

A random number generator, also known as an arbitrary precision random number generator, allows for the generation of numbers within a wide range of values, from a large primorial base. In this study, we evaluate and compare the "randomness" or suitability of two methods for combining and refining these primorial base values, one each from Ansari and Steiner. Our analysis covers both individual and multi-stage approaches, with a focus on compression and information-theoretic properties. Our findings show that both methods demonstrate high-level "good" randomness, but when paired with a an additional specialized function, one of the bases significantly outperforms the other, utilizing a relatively small number of high-entropy values, whereas the other requires a larger collection of mostly low-entropy values. Our testing confirms the advantages of the Ansari method in real-world applications, including notable improvements in compression and key size reductions for cryptographic use cases.

To accurately model and analyze cement-based materials properly, it is crucial to consider the pore fluid's influence on geophysical measurements, which rely heavily on dielectric properties. Pore fluids can significantly alter results, especially in complex materials like cement paste, which expose pores at a wide range of scales. Studies have frequently used deionized water as a reference pore fluid in numerical simulations, although this simplification may not always be valid. To better understand and represent dielectric properties in cement-based materials, this research aimed to determine and compare the dielectric constants of deionized water, tap water, and cement paste at different ages. We found that tap water conforms more closely to the dielectric characteristics of cement paste, which is consistent with the findings of previous studies.

To facilitate the analysis of B-meson decay widths, we've extended OpenFlavor to include a novel class of Wilson coefficients that accommodates heavy-heavy clusters in the theory's Lagrangian. The inclusion of these coefficients has been implemented within the context of two-dimensional strong-coupling gauge theories, specifically in systems featuring digraphs and two-vertex clusters in SU(3) Yang-Mills theory. The obtained results will be utilized to establish a systematic framework for calculating B-meson decay widths.

The use of small drones in a military context is becoming increasingly common, with various countries utilizing them for reconnaissance, combat, targeting, and propaganda purposes. Factors contributing to the advancement of drone technology in different nations can be difficult to determine, especially when communicating such information poses risks to their security. By analyzing publicly available sources, including news articles and government reports, the advantages of each country's drone capabilities can be identified. This paper utilizes natural language processing techniques to gather information on military swarm drones from available sources, focusing on factors such as targeting, surveillance, and information dissemination. By leveraging AI-powered tools to process text based information, the research aims to provide accurate insights on the progress of drone technology in various countries, including Germany, China, Russia, the United States, and Israel.

The information contained in the correlation structure of the IoniZing Gas along our line of sight is leveraged to constrain baryon acoustic oscillations and natural spline correlation functions in the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, ultimately enabling a precise determination of the Hubble constant and key cosmological parameters. By incorporating data from Bebek et al. (2020) and combining it with Planck satellite data, our analysis yields $H_0=69.1^{+1.3}_{-1.5}$ km/s/Mpc and $r_s=5.37^{+0.17}_{-0.19}$ Mpc. Our findings demonstrate that Lyman-$\alpha$ correlation data can pinpoint the Hubble constant with an error margin of less than 3%, surpassing the precision achieved by the Hubble Space Telescope's final data release, Bebek et al. (2020).

Researchers at Fermilab have successfully conducted an experiment where charged particles switch certain properties: horizontal and longitudinal 'wobbly paths' are exchanged between different accelerating stages. This groundbreaking study demonstrated the transfer of emittances, a concept that had previously only been studied through computer simulations. The experiment was carried out with a specific type of particle, negative ions, within a specially designed setup, leveraging the 'electron lens effect' to facilitate emittance transfer: an intense beam of electrons interacts with a test particle, creating an electromagnetic force that affects its trajectory. Analyses of data from the experiment confirmed our understanding of emittance transfer, but also revealed potential areas for further improvement. The success of this study paves the way for future research on emittance exchange, which could lead to innovative advancements in particle accelerators, including more efficient beam transportation and potentially more accurate particle physics experiments at the Fermilab accelerator complex.

This research tackles the challenge of predicting and forecasting future trajectories of multiple entities in crowded spaces. The proposed approach, named SSR-CVAE, incorporates a novel method based on the categorical variational autoencoder type of model. This innovative method considers two key factors: the dynamic nature of object interactions that shape trajectory development, and the incorporation of socially aware re-evaluation of predictions to guarantee a realistic and respectful forecast. The social aspect of our model is represented by the'social mask' which ensures a realistic and respectful forecast. The proposed approach also includes a fully convolutional encoder to reduce dimensionality and a categorical transformer decoder to generate future trajectories. Experimental evaluations using the NuScenes and Argoverne datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in producing more realistic and socially conscious trajectory predictions compared to existing models.

Deep learning networks, essentially complex devices composed of interconnected components called neurons, utilize complex data processing mechanisms that mirror the structure of the human brain. Researchers have suggested various measures to quantify the complexity of such systems, including information-theoretic measures that can be calculated from training data. This study compares three measures of complexity for low-dimensional binary networks, specifically Boltzmann machines. These complexity measures - total information, information increase, and self information - were calculated using training data from networks with varying numbers of neurons. The analysis found that these measures often contradict each other and that total information and self information exhibit contrasting behavior in response to parameter adjustments. This distinction has significant implications for assessing the capacity of such systems to model complex patterns.

This research proposes a novel method for hand motion recognition in dynamic video streams using deep learning techniques. Our approach integrates a Long Short-Term Memory network with a K-Nearest Neighbor algorithm for spatial feature extraction, enabling the tracking of hand positions within scenes. We have optimized the model's structure and training efficiency using a database of simulated hand movements. When tested on the NTU RGB+D dataset, our method demonstrated a 97% accuracy rate for individual frame predictions and a 95% accuracy rate for continuous sequence predictions, despite significant occlusion and varying hand poses. We plan to apply this research to the development of real-time interaction between humans and swarm systems.

The study aims to enhance the accuracy of image classification for blood cells by integrating various neural network models, a technique known as model merging. When multiple models are combined, the outcomes are more stable and less prone to overfitting. This approach allows the identification of the most effective components of each model, enabling the optimization of a new model's architecture. Our paper compares the performance of a new model, built by integrating existing ones, against individual models, as well as a random forest classifier, to evaluate options for a baseline on the blood cell image dataset.

In quantum engineering, rapidly transforming an initial quantum state into a target state with precise control is called counterdiabatic steering. This study introduces a new method, variational counterdiabatic steering, to accomplish this by leveraging counterdiabatic forces and variational principles. It is demonstrated that this approach can be used to drive the Hubbard model towards its ground state with minimal interference during state evolution. The method is capable of adapting to different initial states and can be implemented efficiently with current technologies. The study provides an in-depth analysis of the underlying physical mechanisms, and experiments confirm that variational counterdiabatic steering effectively drives the Hubbard model towards its ground state.

This study introduces a novel empirical model called HUE-Temp for instantly transforming image hues to match their local tonal variations in temperature, specifically within the range of 3700K to 6500K, thereby allowing for high-velocity color deformation. By modifying the hue component in an image according to a linearly progressing temperature formula that incorporates the image's chroma values, the proposed HUE-Temp model effectively simulates the effects of interactions between light rays and atmospheric particles at different temperatures. By comparing the results with other mathematical models and an image processing algorithm, we found that HUE-Temp produces comparable outcomes, but with a key distinction in color deformation, rather than simply shifting tones. Furthermore, HUE-Temp allows for effortless manipulation of input parameters, such as hue velocity and temperature, to achieve various effects, making it an ideal choice for applications such as image processing, computer vision, and machine learning, especially in scenarios where fast parameter adjustments are essential.

This research develops an exponential series expression for the Taylor expansion of $e^{ax}$, where $a$ is a complex number and $x$ is a real variable. Using the established expansion, we derive an explicit formula for the coefficients of $axl$. The formula facilitates the analysis of the convergence domain of the expansion by applying the Absolute Convergence Test. Ultimately, we validate the expansion's convergence in various domains.

Given a surface equipped with a CAT($k$) metric and a multiply connected core, we develop a fundamental harmonic extension theorem, which ensures the existence of a harmonic function extending from the core to the entire surface while remaining constant on the core. Moreover, this extension meets a specific mean-value condition related to the core's topology. Building upon this extension theorem and a key observation involving the Hahn-Banach theorem, we establish the sufficiency of branch points for the harmonic extension of Beltrami operators. Ultimately, these findings combine to prove the existence and uniqueness of the Beltrami operator's harmonic extensions in the presence of specified topological constraints, leading to the uniformization of the given surface via a distortion function.

A new research area called photon-photon science is rapidly gaining traction as a primary tool for studying high-energy density environments, the creation of which was previously solely dependent on the study of relativistic laser-plasma interactions. Laser-plasma sources are now poised to play a pivotal role in this burgeoning field, given their capacity to produce high-energy photons through three mechanisms: the decay of excited atoms, the Breit-Wheeler process, and the direct interaction of high-energy electrons with target matter. We discuss the progress made in utilizing laser-plasma sources for photon-photon interactions over the past decade, highlighting the advancements in experiment design, the increased accessibility of relevant S-shaped photon energy curves, and the comprehensive analytical tools for evaluating the performance of laser-plasma sources within this field. We estimate that approximately 40% of hadron collider waste photons could suffice for a significant increase in luminosity, as well as demonstrate that future large-scale laser facilities are likely to generate a substantial number of photons on the order of $10^{12}$ per second, given their energy outputs exceed 100 megawatts. We conclude by identifying the primary challenges hindering large-scale photon-photon facilities based on laser-plasma sources and proposing potential solutions to overcome these obstacles.

A thorough examination of various characteristics in Type-II two Higgs doublet models with different methods of breaking the $Z_2$ symmetry is conducted, including a random sampling approach. The analysis is based on a given mass $f$ and a specific mass range $m_{12}$, ensuring the presence of necessary conditions for a desired range of $\tan\beta$. Several scenarios are considered, including constraints based on flavor changes and decoherence effects in order to determine the impact of these factors on breaking the $Z_2$ symmetry. The study reveals that while responsivity varies across different scenarios, the model with broken $Z_2$ symmetry and a specific mass range in mind is less effective when considering multiple methods of breaking the symmetry.

The shift towards Semantic Web is significantly driven by the adoption of RDF data. To fully realize this shift, quadrupling the current size is required, necessitating a more efficient approach to converting existing data to RDF. This paper presents a unified approach to this data conversion, facilitated by incorporating Shape Expressions. This innovative method employs Shape Expressions to define the structure of XML/relational data, allowing it to be reconstructed as valid RDF statements. The process of converting data from a relational database to RDF is detailed, including a demonstration of numerous examples that highlight its effectiveness. Additionally, the method has been implemented as an open-source tool, available for public use. This contribution offers a method to automate the conversion of relational data to RDF, particularly beneficial for large datasets, while also providing valuable insights for developers to manually convert such data.

Stochastic nonconvex optimization techniques, like StoNED, enable the analysis of nonconvex functions by taking measurements at randomly selected, non-convexly distributed points. Building on the stoNED method, PyStoNED introduces Python tools for solving convex regression and boundary estimation problems derived from such nonconvex measurements.

In the standard model, the Higgs field is responsible for giving mass to fundamental particles, and its study has been complex due to the challenging nature of detecting the Higgs boson itself. Notably, a subtle Higgs search that utilizes $t \bar t \phi$ production at the LHC has significant potential to complement existing searches for the Higgs boson. This study presents an in-depth analysis of the theoretical underpinnings of the $t \bar t \phi$ search, which includes an extensive examination of background processes and signal paths. Notably, this research demonstrates how to apply topological constraints and kinematic variables to effectively identify the signal. Using MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO, a next-to-leading order simulation of the $t \bar t \phi$ process and subsequent hadronization is performed, and the detector response is accounted for using FastJet. Utilizing the ATLAS detector at 14 TeV, this research finds that the $t \bar t \phi$ search offers sensitivity to the Higgs boson's coupling with top quarks and Higgs production in specific phases space regions, and future analyses can enhance this sensitivity further.

The accuracy of German speech-to-text systems can be enhanced by leveraging open-source Kaldi tools, which are easily integrable into existing projects, including CMU Pronunciation Dictionary, a widely used data set. After installing Kaldi and aligning it with the CPD data set, the resulting closed vocabulary HMM can be used directly in speech recognition applications, offering improved performance compared to systems utilizing other closed vocabulary models. Notably, our improved model, which we refer to as cmu-ws, exhibits a 10% increase in accuracy and surpasses the accuracy of a state-of-the-art, commercially available German speech recognition system in our experiments.

The young, massive star cluster 30 Doradus in the Large Magellanic Cloud is a dynamic growth area for the study of early stellar evolution.
The analysis presented here focuses on spectral data from BEXCESS/Keck II and HIRES/Keck I for 106 Be stars within 30 Doradus, with a larger subset of 213 Galactic Be stars serving as a comparison.
By classifying these stars into distinct spectral subtypes and determining their continuum and absolute magnitudes in the K band, a comprehensive understanding of their shape and mass is gained.
The resulting data reveal several notable patterns.
Firstly, a significant correlation is found between the mass of type B5V-B9V stars and their projected rotation rate, suggesting a rotational cutoff around 20 km/s.
Additionally, a distinction is observed in the rotation rates of type B0V-B5V stars from those in the Galaxy, with the former rotating faster and reaching higher rates.
The effect of the Initial Mass Function on the samples is also discussed, with a cut-off at 8-9 M_{} solar mass mass proposed for sample 30 Doradus.
The study further explores the distribution of type B0V-B5V and type B5V-B9V subtypes, with the former exhibiting a double-horned pattern and both exhibiting skewness towards lower rotation rates.
The study also sheds light on the Be stars' X-ray emission, with a correlation found between X-ray luminosity

Inverse text standardization is a crucial task in natural language processing that involves adjusting text to conform to a target standard, commonly known as ASCII format, while preserving grammatical structure and semantic meaning to facilitate text processing and machine learning. This study addresses the challenge of converting non-ASCII text to ASCII format without losing its meaning. To overcome this challenge, it's essential to maintain the text's semantic and structural integrity, including tokenization, part-of-speech, syntactic, and semantic characteristics. This paper explores various input formats, including tokenized, segmented, and char-based inputs, and proposes a data augmentation approach to boost the performance of models handling these inputs. The experiments showcase the effectiveness of this augmentation method in achieving higher accuracy in converting text to ASCII format.

This document presents a sharp inequality involving the first eigenvalue of the Hermite operator when subjected to Robin boundary conditions. The operators in question are defined on a bounded area within n-dimensional space (where n is 3 or greater), and their edges meet the specified conditions. The study involves demonstrating a quantitative Faber-Krahn inequality, which asserts that the eigenvalue is minimized when the enclosed area is a standard symmetric shape. The standard shape is a ball in cases involving fewer than 8 dimensions, a truncated cone in 7-dimensional space, or other more intricately shaped structures in 3-dimensional and 6-dimensional space. Furthermore, a corresponding inequality involving the first eigenvalue of the Laplace operator on a similar area is also provided, along with a numerical demonstration of the shapes that minimize the eigenvalues in lower dimensions.

Tangent kernel methods build sophisticated Gaussian process models from simpler
combination rules by maximizing their coordinate-wise freedoms to the extent
possible. In this direction, we propose non-exchangeable tangent kernels which
combine the simplicity of mixture priors with the modeling capabilities of
gaussian processes that capture dependencies, through a more flexible distribution
of frequencies in data sets. We demonstrate that such frequencies fall
naturalistically within the data distribution and show a straightforward training
method that locks in optimal frequencies, resulting in a more capable model.
Our core technical contribution is a general framework for choosing the number of
components in non-exchangeable tangent kernels based on data distribution properties
and we propose two specific methods for this choice. Our proposed method is then
evaluated on several datasets, including well-known benchmarks and a few newly
created ones in different domains, where we find that non-exchangeable tangent
kernels offer a more capable model class compared to both mixture priors and
exchangeable Gaussian processes, with the added benefit of simpler computational
requirements.

Recent studies indicate that non-Hermitian systems possess unique periodic characteristics, which arise from non-linear equations and distinct "glowing" spacial regions. However, in recent experiments and simulations, a significant variation of non-Hermitian systems has been observed, where these unique features vanish and replace with random, disordered behavior within specific areas. Our research explores a one-dimensional non-Hermitian system where this disappearance of "glowing" properties occurs due to correlations and internal resistance. Our analysis, incorporating both theoretical and numerical methods, reveals a significant link between the system's features and the emergence of "glowing" regions within specific areas, where these unique features vanish and replace with random, disordered behavior on the opposite sides. Our findings also demonstrate that this disappearance of "glowing" properties is influenced by correlations and internal resistance. Our research opens new avenues in studying a specific model of non-Hermitian systems where "glowing" properties are impacted by correlations and internal resistance. Our analysis, a combination of topological features and the effects of correlations and internal resistance, provides a comprehensive understanding of "glowing" properties in non-Hermitian systems. Our research opens new avenues in studying a specific model of non-Hermitian systems where "glowing" properties are impacted by correlations and internal resistance.

Currently, social speaker characteristics like personality, emotional intelligence, and cultural background are not fully represented in high-quality speech synthesis systems. To address this, a significant study is conducted to understand how to effectively integrate these social traits into synthesized speech, while ensuring that the resulting speech appears more authentic and engaging. To achieve this, a comprehensive framework is developed, which involves identifying relevant social traits, defining their expected expressions, categorizing these expressions, and training an advanced model to bring these social traits to life within synthesized speech. A custom-made database is also created, containing recordings of individuals conveying distinct emotions, as part of a broader effort to provide the world with more diverse and relatable spoken content.

A theoretical model combining features of the Standard Model and Zee-type bosonic dark matter has been proposed within the framework of a modified version of $U(1)_{B-L}$ extended Standard Model. This involves incorporating a fundamental modular symmetry in the model, which allows for the creation of bosonic dark matter composed of exotic particles such as $\sigma$, $\rho$, and $\omega$. The inclusion of modular group $A_4$ symmetry gives rise to a pattern of vacuum expectation values for scalar fields, which goes beyond the most conventional configurations. As a result, dark matter consists of various possible combinations of particles, such as $\langle \sigma \rangle^3$, $\langle \rho \rangle^3$, and $\langle \omega \rho \rangle$. Furthermore, dark matter can also emerge from the possible combinations of these fields, which are constrained by conditions derived from the modular group $A_4$ symmetry. The model's predictions for the luminous dark matter density are calculated, which are then compared to existing observations and future projections, specifically the ones planned for the CRESST experiment, which utilizes cryogenic detectors to study potential interactions between WIMPs and crystals. The findings indicate that while the standard model's relic density is generally consistent with current data and future experiments, it is largely independent of the model parameters. However, this does not apply to the luminous dark matter contribution, which is heavily dependent on specific conditions and constraints derived from the model's symmetries and

In light of the minimal length concept rooted in the modified Hagedorn structure theory, a novel quantum model has been developed for triaxial nuclei, incorporating the Crank-Nicholson algorithm for solving the single-particle Riemann-based Hamiltonian. This model's key objective is to determine whether the single-particle quantum spectrum is capable of capturing the collective movement characteristics of axially symmetric nuclei, such as $^{120}$Te, without recourse to the Bohr-Mottelson theory. In an effort to achieve this goal, a numerical solution is sought to the modified Hamiltonian, conditioned on the single parameter, minimal length. In addition to exploring the single-particle spectrum, this solution aims to investigate the derived two-body spectra in its entirety. In a comparative analysis, this work also computes the point-coupling effective interaction (V$_{6}$) matrix elements, based on the Zel'dovich formalism, in an attempt to shed light on the underlying physics of triaxial nuclei. Ultimately, this work's numerical results reveal that the single-particle spectrum derived from the minimal length concept bears striking resemblance to that predicted by the Riemann Hamiltonian, while also closely approximating the measured spectra obtained via Gogny-HF+RDBE methods. In an effort to validate its effectiveness, this model's ability to describe collective movements in triaxial nuclei is also tested through the computation of various RDBE parameters.
